title: Write the rule
hook: one page, kept where you'll see it
tomorrow: what was the very first prayer this path taught you?

segments.voice: Yesterday: adjusting with the seasons, and the line it bends, not breaks, a monastery that naps in summer. A rule that bends still has to be written somewhere.

A sticky note on a mirror. Three words on a lock screen. A coach's game plan on one laminated card. Some things are written so you can't miss them. The prophet Habakkuk is told to do exactly that, in the Douay-Rheims: "Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables: that he that readeth it may run over it." Run? Why would a prophet write so a runner could read it?
screen: `A NOTE ON THE MIRROR.` → `WRITE THE VISION, MAKE IT PLAIN.` → `WHY WOULD A READER RUN?`

segments.voice: Some readers take it this way: write it so large and plain that someone running past can take it in at a glance. Others read it as: so the one who reads it can run, carrying the message on. Either way, the vision isn't buried in a long scroll. It's short, plain and out where people pass. Moses says the same about God's words: "thou shalt write them in the entry, and on the doors of thy house." One to tell a friend: Jewish tradition keeps that verse with a mezuzah, a small case on the doorpost holding those very words. Benedict asked that his Rule be read aloud often, so no one could say he didn't know it. A rule you can't remember can't guide you. That's where this stretch lands. Fifteen days built a rule: what already works, a time and place to pray, Sunday at the center, a rhythm for confession, scripture daily, regular mercy, a book, your people, a guide, a little hunger, a portion, holy leisure, company for the road, and a rule that bends. Now it goes on one page. One short line each, plain enough to read on the run.
screen: `WRITE THE VISION, MAKE IT PLAIN.` · `SO A RUNNER CAN READ IT.` · `ON THE DOORS OF THY HOUSE.` · `FIFTEEN DAYS, ONE PAGE.` · then, large: `ONE PAGE.`

segments.voice: Take one sheet of paper and write your rule, one short line per piece: when you pray, Sunday, confession, a reading, service, a book, your people, a guide, a fast, a portion, rest, a saint. If a line runs long, shrink it. Then fold the page once and decide where it will live.
Write the rule. Fifteen days of pieces on one plain page, kept where you'll pass it every day.
Keep this: one page, plain enough to read on the run, and yours now. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Catholics who keep a personal rule of life often write it on a single page or card, review it with a confessor or spiritual director, and revisit it at the start of Advent or Lent.

fork.reveal: Moses said write them in the entry, on the doors: where you pass. who else sees it matters less than whether you do.

chat.meaning: Habakkuk was told to make the vision plain enough to read on the run. One page you pass every day guides you; three you skip don't.

Habakkuk.meaning: a prophet of Israel with a short book in the Old Testament

Moses.meaning: the prophet who led Israel out of Egypt and gave God's law

mezuzah.meaning: a small case on a Jewish doorpost holding verses from Deuteronomy

Benedict.meaning: an Italian monk and saint who wrote a Rule for monasteries

confession.meaning: the sacrament of penance: telling sins to a priest and receiving absolution
